content_json.html: How do we assemble a single-channel ECG device?
content_json.title: What would you like to learn about?

content_json.html: The simplest process in assembling a single-channel ECG device is developing a way to obtain reliable information about the functioning of the human heart for medical purposes.
content_json.title: The need to measure the ECG signal leads to the creation of an instrument
Developing a method for measuring the electrical activity of the heart

content_json.html:
To obtain information about how the heart works, we need to determine which manifestations allow us to assess its condition.

As the heart works, the heart muscle contracts, blood moves, sounds occur, and electrical changes take place. Blood movement can be used to assess the pulse, and sounds can reveal certain aspects of how the heart works. Each method provides particular information.

Since our task is to assemble a single-channel ECG device, we choose to study the electrical activity of the heart. Electrical changes in the heart muscle are associated with the onset and spread of excitation, which causes it to contract. By studying the sequence of these changes, we can assess heart rhythm and certain disturbances in heart function.

However, electrical processes take place inside the heart. To study them, we need to establish how they manifest themselves beyond the heart muscle and what exactly we will be able to measure.
content_json.title: Moving from ways of studying the heart to studying electrical activity
content_json.author: ai_checked

content_json.html:
Electrically charged particles—ions—are found inside and around heart cells. They are distributed unevenly. When ions move through the cell membrane, the distribution of electric charges changes. This change can trigger a similar process in neighboring cells. This is how electrical excitation spreads through the heart muscle, causing it to contract.

Since different parts of the heart are not excited simultaneously, differences in electric potential arise between them. These cause electric currents in the surrounding tissues, which conduct electricity. As a result, the electrical activity of the heart also manifests itself on the surface of the skin: a small potential difference arises between different points and changes as the heart works.

Thus, we can obtain information about the electrical activity of the heart by measuring changes in voltage between points on the surface of the skin. We now need to determine which specific points to choose and how to carry out the measurement.
content_json.title: Moving from the electrical activity of the heart to an electrical signal
content_json.author: ai_checked

content_json.html:
Electrical excitation does not affect the entire heart muscle simultaneously, but spreads sequentially from one group of cells to another. This spreading change in the electrical state of cells is called a wave of excitation.

As the wave spreads, the distribution of electric potentials on the surface of the body changes. These changes manifest themselves differently at different points. The measurement result therefore depends on which points we use to determine the potential difference.

To begin with, we choose two points corresponding to the right and left arms. By measuring the change in potential difference between them over time, we obtain one of the standard ECG leads—lead I.

To transmit electric potentials from the selected areas of skin to the measuring device, we need conductive contacts. These contacts are called electrodes.

We have now determined exactly which electrical signal we want to measure and where to obtain it. However, to record it, we need to find out how to transmit this weak signal to the measuring device without distorting it or endangering the person.
content_json.title: Choosing points for measuring the heart's electrical signal
content_json.author: ai_checked

content_json.html:
We have chosen two points on the surface of the skin between which we will measure the electric potential difference. To transmit these potentials to the measuring device, we place electrodes at these points and connect each electrode to the corresponding input of the device using a conductor.

An electronic circuit must operate inside the device to compare the voltages at the two inputs and record their difference. Electronic components require electrical energy to operate, so the device is connected to a power source.

Thus, we connect the human body to an electrical system that has its own voltages and carries electric currents. Although the current through the body should be very small during normal measurement, a fault or insulation failure may allow electric current to pass through the electrodes and the human body.

It turns out that the electrical connection needed to obtain information about how the heart works also creates the possibility of a dangerous effect on the person. We now need to find out what this danger consists of.
content_json.title: Connecting the human body to an electrical measuring device
content_json.author: ai_checked

rejected_drafts.html:
We have chosen two points on the surface of the skin between which we will measure the electric potential difference. However, the measuring device is separate from these points. We therefore need to ensure that the electrical signal is transmitted from each electrode to the corresponding input of the device.

To do this, we connect each electrode to a separate input of the measuring device using an insulated conductor. The device can now compare the voltages at the two electrodes and determine their difference, which changes as the heart works.

However, the measurement itself may affect the voltage being measured. If electric current flows through the device's inputs, some voltage is lost across the resistance of the skin and contacts. Therefore, the measuring device must have a high input impedance so that it has virtually no effect on the signal being measured.

In addition, the conductors may pick up electrical interference that is superimposed on the weak ECG signal. We now need to find out how to measure a small voltage difference while reducing the effect of this interference.
rejected_drafts.reason: The AI tried to move away from the topic of "electrical instrument–human safety," that is, from the contradiction, to details of the instrument that should be addressed later. It did so as follows: "We now need to find out how to measure a small voltage difference while reducing the effect of this interference."

content_json.html:
The functioning of the heart, nerves, and muscles is associated with changes in electric potentials in their cells. Electric current passing through the tissues of the human body can therefore interfere with these processes: it can cause involuntary muscle contractions and disrupt breathing and heart rhythm.

For current to pass through the body, it must become part of a closed electrical circuit. If a fault in the instrument causes the voltage of its power source to be applied to the electrodes, electric current may flow through the human body.

The danger depends on the current magnitude, the duration of exposure, its path through the body, and its frequency. Under certain conditions, even a relatively small current can disrupt heart function.

Thus, a device intended to obtain information about the heart can itself disrupt its functioning. The more we seek to use an electrical connection to study the heart, the more important it becomes to prevent this connection from having a dangerous effect on the person.

Ensuring human safety now becomes a necessary condition for the medical use of ECG, while also limiting the chosen measurement method.
content_json.title: Discovering the danger of electric current to humans
content_json.author: ai_checked

content_json.html:
We are creating a device to obtain information about how the heart works in order to help people maintain their health. However, we have found that, under certain conditions, electric current from the device itself can harm a person, including by disrupting heart function.

To prevent such harm, we need to rule out the passage of dangerous electric current through the human body. If the safety of connecting the instrument has not been confirmed, we have to refrain from connecting it, even if this makes it impossible to obtain an ECG signal.

Thus, the medical purpose for which we are creating the electrocardiograph also limits the use of the chosen measurement method.

At the same time, ensuring human safety does not depend on the existence of ECG. It is necessary even in the absence of any medical measurements.

Thus, as the method of obtaining information about the heart develops, an opposing process emerges—ensuring human safety, which may require abandoning the electrical measurement itself.
content_json.title: The need to ensure human safety arises
content_json.author: ai_checked

content_json.html:
Ensuring human safety is aimed at preventing effects that could harm a person's health and life. This process exists independently of ECG measurement.

Under certain conditions, electric current can disrupt the functioning of the muscles, nervous system, and heart. Ensuring safety therefore requires preventing dangerous electrical effects on the body. If the safety of an electrical device has not been confirmed, connecting it to a person is unacceptable.

However, health is threatened not only by external effects but also by disturbances in the functioning of the heart itself. To detect such disturbances in time, we need to obtain information about cardiac activity. ECG is one way to obtain it.

Thus, ensuring human safety both requires the use of ECG to identify possible diseases and prevents the use of an electrocardiograph if its electrical effects could harm the person.
content_json.title: The opposing process—ensuring human safety
content_json.author: ai_checked

content_json.html:
We must create a device that measures the electrical activity of the heart and allows us to obtain information about how it works. However, such a device must not be connected to a person until its safety has been checked.

To begin assembly, we need an electrical signal that can be measured without involving a person. Furthermore, the characteristics of this signal must be known in advance; otherwise, we will not be able to determine whether the instrument being created is working correctly.

To do this, we reproduce the electrical changes characteristic of heart function using a special device—an ECG simulator. It generates an electrical voltage that changes over time, which we will supply to the measurement input of the instrument being assembled.

Thus, we can begin creating a single-channel ECG device and check measurement results without putting a person in danger. At the same time, we are assembling one instrument and using the simulator only to test it.

We now need to determine what the reproduced signal should be like so that it can be used to check the operation of the future electrocardiograph.
content_json.title: Beginning to assemble the instrument without connecting it to a person
content_json.author: ai_checked

content_json.html:
Electrical excitation spreads through the heart muscle from one group of cells to another. This spreading change in electrical state is called a wave of excitation. As it moves, the electric potential difference between selected points on the surface of the body changes.

If we measure this difference sequentially and plot the resulting values on a graph, we will see how the voltage increases, decreases, and changes sign. This produces the characteristic waves of the electrocardiogram, reflecting different stages of the electrical activity of the heart. With each heartbeat, the sequence of these changes usually repeats.

To check the instrument being created, we need to know in advance what signal it should record. We therefore select an ECG waveform on the simulator and set the heart rate to 60 beats per minute. This means that one cardiac cycle will repeat every second. We set the amplitude of the test signal to 1 mV, thereby specifying the magnitude of its deviation from the baseline.

We now know how the signal should change over time and what voltage values we expect to obtain. However, the simulator itself only generates these changes. To obtain a cardiogram, we need to measure them and save the results.
content_json.title: Reproducing an artificial ECG signal
content_json.author: ai_checked

content_json.html:
The ECG simulator generates an electrical voltage that changes continuously over time. To obtain a cardiogram from it, we need to measure this voltage and save the results. However, a continuously changing voltage cannot be stored directly in a digital device's memory: it must first be represented as numbers.

To do this, we connect the simulator outputs corresponding to the selected lead to two measurement inputs of the future electrocardiograph. The electronic circuit determines the voltage difference between them at discrete moments in time. Each such measured value is called a sample.

To reproduce the ECG waveform, measurements must be repeated at equal time intervals. For example, at a rate of 500 measurements per second, 2 milliseconds elapse between consecutive samples. This is the signal's sampling rate, not the heart rate.

The resulting voltage must be converted into a number. This task is performed by an analog-to-digital converter—an ADC. It assigns a digital value to the measured voltage within the set range. A bit depth of 16 bits allows 65 536 different numerical levels. However, measurement accuracy depends not only on their number but also on the quality of the measurement circuit itself.

Thus, instead of a continuous electrical signal, we obtain a sequence of numbers, each corresponding to a particular moment in time. These data can be used to reconstruct the cardiogram's waveform on a graph.

We now need to choose an electronic circuit capable of measuring small ECG voltages and converting them into digital values.
content_json.title: Turning an electrical signal into a sequence of numbers
content_json.author: ai_checked

content_json.html:
We have learned to represent an electrical signal as a sequence of numbers. Now we need to create an electronic circuit that will perform this conversion.

The ECG signal is very small. For example, a voltage of 1 mV is only one thousandth of a volt. At the same time, external electrical signals can affect both measurement inputs simultaneously. We therefore need a circuit that extracts the voltage difference between the inputs, attenuates identical changes at both inputs as much as possible, and allows small changes in the desired signal to be distinguished.

A differential amplifier is used for this purpose. It specifically amplifies the difference between the input voltages. For example, with a gain of 6, a difference of 1 mV becomes 6 mV. However, excessive amplification can cause the signal to exceed the measurement range and distort its shape.

To avoid assembling an amplifier and an ADC from separate components, we choose the specialized ADS1291 chip from Texas Instruments. It combines an amplifier with adjustable gain and a 24-bit ADC. It is designed to measure weak electrical signals, including ECG signals, and can provide 500 digital samples per second.

Thus, we have chosen the basis for the measurement section of a single-channel electrocardiograph. But the chip itself is not yet a working device: it needs electrical power, additional components, and a device that will receive the measurement results. Having a specialized chip also does not mean that the device is already safe to connect to a person.
content_json.title: Choosing an integrated circuit for ECG measurement
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Texas Instruments — ADS1291, ADS1292, ADS1292R Datasheet (Rev. C).
sources.quote: Official technical documentation for the ADS1291 measurement chip. Contains descriptions of the amplifier, 24-bit ADC, gain ranges, sampling rate, electrical characteristics, and component connection requirements. Main sections to study: 1, 6.5

content_json.html:
We have chosen the ADS1291 chip, which can convert changes in electrical voltage into a sequence of numbers. However, it does not create an ECG recording on its own. We need to control the measurement process, receive each number, store it, and transmit it to plot the ECG trace.

To perform these actions, we need a small computer that runs a previously stored program. Such a computer, whose main parts are contained within a single chip, is called a microcontroller.

A microcontroller contains a processor, memory, and electronic devices for exchanging signals with external components. The processor executes instructions. One area of memory stores the program that determines the sequence of actions, while another stores the data the processor is currently working with. A built-in clock generator sets the operating rhythm of the electronic circuits.

When the microcontroller is switched on, the processor begins executing the instructions of the stored program. It reads them from memory in sequence, determines the required actions, and performs them. For example, one instruction may write a number to memory, another may check the state of an electrical input, and a third may send data to an output. This is how many simple operations combine to make the device work.

For our electrocardiograph, we must write a program that the microcontroller will use to configure the ADS1291, receive measurement results from it, and store them in the correct sequence. Each result is represented by a set of binary digits—zeros and ones. The microcontroller receives these digits and reconstructs the numerical voltage value from them.

Thus, the ADS1291 will measure and convert the electrical signal, while the microcontroller will control the acquisition and processing of the results. For them to work together, we need to choose a microcontroller and understand how electronic devices exchange digital data.
content_json.title: Organizing measurement control using a microcontroller
content_json.author: ai_checked

content_json.html:
We have chosen the ADS1291 chip to measure electrical voltage and a microcontroller to control the measurements and process their results. Now we need to organize the transfer of information between them.

Electronic devices transmit digital information using electrical signals. Two distinguishable voltage states are used for this purpose and are represented by the digits 0 and 1. Each such digit is called a bit. Any number can be represented in the binary number system by transmitting a sequence of bits. For example, the sequence 1011 represents the number 11.

However, if we simply change the voltage on a wire, the receiving device will not know when to read the next bit. The microcontroller therefore generates a separate clock signal—a sequence of electrical pulses. These pulses allow the timing of data transmission and reception to be coordinated.

The SPI interface is used to exchange information with the ADS1291. It provides separate connections for sending commands from the microcontroller to the ADS1291 (DIN), sending results back (DOUT), the clock signal (SCLK), and selecting the chip for communication (CS). Another signal (DRDY) tells the microcontroller that a new measurement result is ready.

During operation, the microcontroller sends the ADS1291 commands to configure and start measurements. When the next conversion is complete, the ADS1291 indicates that the result is ready. The microcontroller supplies clock pulses, reads the transmitted bits in sequence, and combines them into numerical data. Each voltage measurement result contains 24 bits.

Thus, we have determined how the two main chips in our electrocardiograph will interact. Now we need to choose a specific microcontroller that can perform these actions, store the results, and transmit them for display as an ECG trace.
content_json.title: Organizing data exchange between the microcontroller and the ADS1291
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Texas Instruments — ADS1291, ADS1292, ADS1292R Datasheet (Rev. C).
sources.quote: Section 8.5.1, “SPI Interface,” explains the transmission of commands and measurement results through DIN, DOUT, SCLK, and CS, as well as the purpose of the DRDY ready signal. The communication diagrams show the bit transmission sequence.

content_json.html:
We have determined how the microcontroller should exchange data with the ADS1291. Now we need to choose a specific device that can perform this work.

The microcontroller must support the SPI interface so that it can send commands to the measurement chip and receive measurement results. It also needs memory to store the program and the acquired data. Finally, the results will need to be transmitted to a computer or another device so that the ECG trace can be viewed.

For this purpose, we choose the ESP32-S3 from Espressif. This microcontroller contains a processor, memory, and electronic circuits for exchanging data over SPI. It also supports USB, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth Low Energy, so we will be able to arrange both wired and wireless ECG transmission later on.

However, a standalone microcontroller still needs a power supply, a connection to a computer, and a way to load a program. To avoid assembling all the supporting circuits ourselves at the initial stage, we use the ready-made ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 development board.

This board has a module containing the microcontroller, the necessary supporting components, USB connectors, and pins for connecting other electronic devices.

Thus, we have determined which devices will perform the two main tasks: the ADS1291 will measure the electrical signal and convert it into numbers, while the ESP32-S3 will control the measurements and receive the results.

But the microcontroller does not yet know exactly which actions it needs to perform. For this, we need to create a program and write it to the device's memory. Now we need to understand how such programs are created and how the microcontroller executes them.
content_json.title: Choosing a microcontroller for a single-channel ECG device
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Espressif — ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 v1.1 User Guide.
sources.quote: Official guide to the ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 development board. Describes the board's layout, built-in components, pins, connectors, and options for connecting it to a computer.

content_json.html:
We have chosen the ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 board to control ECG measurements. However, the microcontroller does not know which actions it needs to perform. To define these actions, we must create a program.

A program is a sequence of instructions written according to specific rules. For the ESP32-S3, we will use the C programming language. For example, the program can include an instruction that displays the message “The program is running” on the computer screen. We can also specify that actions should be repeated at certain time intervals or that an instruction should be executed when a signal arrives from another device.

But the microcontroller's processor does not understand program text written in C. It executes machine instructions represented by binary numbers. The written program must therefore be converted using a special software tool—a compiler. Together with other build tools, it creates a file containing the instructions and data needed for the microcontroller to operate.

To prepare the program, we use ESP-IDF—a set of development tools provided by the manufacturer of the ESP32-S3. On the computer, we create a project, write the program, and build it. We then connect the development board to the computer via USB and load the resulting file into the board's nonvolatile flash memory, where the program remains stored even after the power is turned off.

When the microcontroller is switched on, a utility program starts and initiates execution of the loaded application. The processor begins executing its machine instructions. For example, when it receives an instruction to display a message, it transmits the corresponding data through the communication interface with the computer.

Let us test this with the simplest program: load it into the ESP32-S3 and make sure that the message “The program is running” appears in the computer's terminal window. This will confirm that we can create, load, and run programs on the chosen microcontroller.

Now we can move from executing individual instructions to controlling the ADS1291: sending it settings, starting measurements, and receiving digital values of the ECG signal.
content_json.title: Creating and loading the microcontroller program
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Espressif — Start a Project on Windows from Command Line.
sources.quote: Official instructions for programming the ESP32-S3 in Windows using ESP-IDF. Shows how to create a project using the Hello World example, compile the program, load it into the board's memory via USB, and check the result in the terminal.

stickers.text: The code itself is not provided.

content_json.html:
We have learned to create and load a program into the ESP32-S3 microcontroller. Now we need to use this program to control the ADS1291 so that it starts measuring voltage and transmitting the acquired values.

The microcontroller cannot simply send the ADS1291 a text instruction saying “measure voltage.” The chip recognizes specific sequences of zeros and ones to which the manufacturer has assigned specific actions in advance. Such sequences are called commands.

In addition to commands, the ADS1291 uses registers—small areas of memory inside the chip intended to store settings and information about its status. For example, the CONFIG1 register determines the rate at which measurement results are obtained, while the CH1SET register determines the measurement channel settings, including signal gain.

To begin, we include a communication check in the program. The microcontroller will send the SDATAC command, which stops continuous data output mode, and then the RREG command to read the ID register. In response, the ADS1291 should transmit a number that can be used to identify the chip type. If the response matches the documentation, we will have our first confirmation that data exchange is working correctly.

After this, the program must apply the necessary measurement settings. In the CONFIG1 register, we select continuous signal conversion at a rate of 500 samples per second. At the clock frequency specified by the manufacturer, the bit combination 010 is used for this. In the CH1SET register, we configure the operation of the first measurement channel and the required gain.

The microcontroller then starts conversion with the START command and enables continuous output of results with the RDATAC command. The ADS1291 performs measurements on its own. When the next conversion is complete, it changes the state of the DRDY output to indicate that new data is ready. The microcontroller reads it over SPI: first the chip status information, then a 24-bit number representing the voltage measurement result.

Thus, we have determined the program's sequence of actions: check communication, configure the measurement, start it, and receive results. But for now, this is only a planned operating sequence. For the program to actually control the ADS1291, we need to connect the two chips, provide them with power, and check that data exchange works correctly on a laboratory test bench without connecting to a person.
content_json.title: Learning to control the ADS1291 measurement chip
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Espressif — SPI Master Driver, ESP32-S3.
sources.quote: Official guide to software control of SPI on the ESP32-S3. Explains how to configure the interface and transmit commands and data to external chips using ESP-IDF.

sources.title: Texas Instruments — ADS129x Low-Power, 2-Channel, 24-Bit Analog Front-End for Biopotential Measurements, Datasheet (Rev. C).
sources.quote: Section 8.3.11 and Figure 44 contain the recommended sequence for initial startup and testing of the ADS1291. Sections 8.5–8.6 describe SPI commands, register settings, the internal reference voltage, and measurement data output. Used to develop and test the ESP32-S3 program.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: starting the ADS1291
stickers.text:
Before the ADS1291 can begin measuring voltage, its internal electronic circuits must be made operational. In addition to electrical power, the chip needs a clock signal that determines its operating rhythm and a reference voltage against which the ADC compares the measured signal.

The ADS1291 contains its own clock generator and reference voltage source. We will use them for the initial check to avoid adding external devices. With an analog supply of 3 V, the internal reference voltage source is set to 2.42 V. It must be enabled and allowed to stabilize.

After preparing the chip, the ESP32-S3 microcontroller sends the SDATAC command over SPI. This stops automatic output of results and allows access to the configuration registers.

First, we check whether the chip responds to commands. To do this, we send RREG with the address of the ID register. The ADS1291 returns a number whose individual bits allow the chip model to be identified. The program compares these bits with the documentation. If the response is incorrect, we must not proceed to measurements: we first need to determine the cause of the error.

We then set the measurement parameters. We write a value corresponding to 500 samples per second to CONFIG1, and in CH1SET we select the mode that internally connects the measurement inputs. This mode allows us to examine the measurement section's own noise without an external signal.

After configuration, we start conversion and enable continuous output of results. When the ADS1291 finishes the next measurement, its DRDY output changes state. The microcontroller detects this change and reads a sequence of six bytes: the first three contain chip status information, and the next three contain the voltage measurement result.

For an additional check, we switch the ADS1291 to its built-in test signal. The chip can generate square-wave voltage oscillations on its own at a frequency of 1 Hz. If the acquired digital values change with the expected frequency and amplitude, this helps confirm the operation of the measurement channel and data exchange.

Thus, we obtain a test sequence: start the chip, check communication, configure measurements, acquire results, and record the internal test signal. Only after these checks does it make sense to move on to an external ECG simulator.

The command sequence has been checked against the manufacturer's documentation, but has not yet been tested on our equipment.

To create a working program, we need to define the physical connections between the ESP32-S3 and the ADS1291, implement communication through the SPI driver, properly organize the enabling of the reference voltage and clock generator, and check compliance with the chip's timing requirements.

In particular, starting the internal test signal does not confirm that the external measurement connections are correct.

All of this applies exclusively to laboratory testing of the electronic system without connecting it to a person.

content_json.html:
We have determined how the ESP32-S3 microcontroller should control the ADS1291 IC, but for now they exist as two separate devices. For them to work together, we need to provide electrical connections and power.

The ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 board already contains the components needed for the microcontroller to operate. However, the ADS1291 is a separate IC with 32 metal pins. Connecting it directly to the development board with ordinary wires is inconvenient. We therefore create a printed circuit board for the ADS1291, on which we will place the IC and the necessary additional components.

First, we draw up a circuit diagram. It shows which component pins should be connected to one another. For measurement, we use the ADS1291 inputs labeled IN1P and IN1N. They are intended to receive two voltages whose difference the IC will measure.

We now need to enable its internal components to operate. The ADS1291 has separate power supply pins for its analog section (AVDD and AVSS) and digital section (DVDD and DGND). The analog section measures a weak electrical signal, while the digital section controls conversion and data transmission. For our circuit, we provide a regulated 3.0 V supply for the analog section and a 3.3 V supply for the digital section, compatible with the ESP32-S3 logic levels.

As electronic components operate, the current they consume changes, which can cause the supply voltage to fluctuate slightly. To reduce the effect of these changes on measurement, we place capacitors near the ADS1291 power supply pins. They can quickly release their stored charge during a brief change in current consumption.

Next, we connect the ADS1291 digital pins to the microcontroller pins: the DIN, DOUT, SCLK, and CS lines provide SPI communication, while DRDY indicates that the next measurement is ready. We also provide the necessary connections for starting and resetting the IC. We select the specific ESP32-S3 pins using the board documentation and implement this choice in the program.

Using the resulting circuit diagram, we design a printed circuit board in KiCad: we place the components and the conductive traces between them. We keep the connections carrying the weak signal being measured away from digital lines that could cause interference.

After checking the circuit diagram, we can manufacture the board and install the components. Before switching on the power, we need to check that the connections are correct and that there are no short circuits.

We have now defined the design of the measurement system. The next step is to test its operation on a laboratory test bench, first without an input signal and then using an ECG simulator. This experimental system must not be connected to a person: its safety has not yet been confirmed.
content_json.title: Creating an electronic measurement board

stickers.text:
The card explains the design principle, but does not yet replace a complete working circuit diagram with all pin numbers, component values, and verification of the protection circuits. For actual assembly, this will need to be prepared separately based on the documentation.

The proposed list of connections describes a preliminary design solution, not a verified working circuit diagram. All connections for unused pins, the values of auxiliary components, the power supply circuit, and the permissible conditions for applying an external signal have not yet been defined.

The exact versions of the ADS1291 and the ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 board also need to be selected. Manufacturing the laboratory board can begin only after the complete design has been checked against the manufacturer's documentation. It is intended exclusively for testing with artificial signals.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: connection diagram for the ADS1291 and ESP32-S3
stickers.text:
To create a laboratory measurement board, we need to define all the connections without which the ADS1291 will not be able to perform measurements and transmit results.

We begin with the power supply. For the analog section, we provide a regulated voltage of 3.0 V between the AVDD and AVSS pins; for the digital section, 3.3 V between DVDD and DGND. These are separate power supply circuits because the measurement and digital sections of the IC perform different tasks. In the laboratory circuit, their common potentials must be aligned so that digital signals are transmitted correctly between the ADS1291 and ESP32-S3.

The next task is to enable the ADC to operate. To use the internal 2.42 V reference voltage, we provide the necessary connections for the VREFP and VREFN pins and auxiliary capacitors. The VREFN pin is connected to AVSS. Capacitors are also required for the VCAP1 and VCAP2 pins, which support the operation of the IC's internal electronic circuits.

To generate clock pulses, we select the ADS1291 internal oscillator. Its operation is determined by the CLKSEL pin. The PWDN/RESET pin allows control of the IC reset, while START controls the start of conversion.
For digital communication between the ADS1291 and ESP32-S3, we provide the following connections.

We connect the ADS1291 DIN pin (19) to GPIO11 of the ESP32-S3 microcontroller. The microcontroller transmits commands over this connection.

We connect the DOUT pin (21) to GPIO13. Through it, the ADS1291 transmits measurement results to the microcontroller.

We connect the SCLK pin (20) to GPIO12. This line carries clock pulses that coordinate the exchange of digital data.

We connect the CS pin (18) to GPIO10. This signal allows the microcontroller to select the ADS1291 for data exchange.

We connect the DRDY pin (22) to GPIO14. A change in this signal tells the microcontroller that a new measurement result is ready.

We connect the PWDN/RESET pin (15) to GPIO8. It is used to control the IC reset.

We connect the START pin (16) to GPIO7. It is intended to control the starting and stopping of conversion.

This is a preliminary connection arrangement. Before manufacturing the board, we need to check the pin numbers and the compatibility of the selected pins against the manufacturers' documentation. The same GPIO numbers must be used in the microcontroller program.

The voltage being measured will be applied to IN1P and IN1N. But simply connecting wires is not enough for operation with an external simulator: we need to make sure that the voltages at both inputs are within the permitted limits relative to the IC's power supply. We will also need to determine how to handle the remaining ADS1291 pins that are not used in the single-channel measurement system.

Thus, we have defined the main connections of the measurement board, but have not yet completed its design. To do this, we need to check all 32 ADS1291 pins against the manufacturer's documentation, select the specified capacitors and other components, determine their values, and develop the final circuit diagram in KiCad.

stickers.title: Operating range of the ADS1291 measurement inputs
stickers.text:
We have determined that the ADS1291 measures the voltage difference between the IN1P and IN1N inputs. However, for correct measurement, it is not enough for the difference itself to be small. We also need to consider the voltage of each input relative to the common power supply point of the measurement circuit.

Suppose the voltage at the first input is 1.501 V and at the second input it is 1.500 V. The difference is 1 mV. The average level of the two voltages is 1.5005 V. This is called the common-mode voltage.

Now imagine that the voltage at the first input is 0.101 V and at the second input it is 0.100 V. The difference remains the same—1 mV—but the average level is now much lower.

The ADS1291 measurement amplifier can operate correctly only within a certain range of common-mode voltages. This range depends on the supply voltage, gain, and magnitude of the signal being measured.

Therefore, when creating the electronic circuit, we need to ensure not only that the required voltage difference is applied, but also that both input voltages are at permissible levels relative to the IC's power supply.

Electrocardiographs may use special bias circuits to control the common-mode level and reduce interference, including the RLD (Right Leg Drive) system provided by the ADS1291.

At the same time, one ECG lead does not necessarily mean using only two electrodes. An additional reference electrode may be used to establish the electrical conditions for measurement without creating a second measured lead.

For our laboratory device, we need to select and verify a specific solution for establishing the operating level of the measurement inputs. It must be coordinated with the measurement and protection sections of the circuit. Until then, the ADS1291 connection diagram cannot be considered complete.

content_json.html:
We have determined how to connect the ADS1291 and ESP32-S3 into a single electronic system. We now need to find out whether it can actually measure an electrical signal and transmit the results to the microcontroller.

After manufacturing and assembling the board under the teacher's supervision, we first check that its electrical connections are correct. With the power disconnected, we use a multimeter to make sure there is no short circuit between the power supply circuits. We then apply the low-voltage power supply specified in the circuit diagram and check its voltage. If deviations are detected, we stop the test until the cause has been eliminated.

Once the power supply has been checked, we load the prepared program into the ESP32-S3. It communicates with the ADS1291 through SPI and reads the ID register. We compare the value obtained with the manufacturer's documentation. A match shows that the microcontroller can exchange digital data with the measurement IC, but does not yet confirm that voltage measurement is correct.

For the next test, we use the test signal generator built into the ADS1291. It allows a periodically changing voltage to be applied to the measurement section of the IC without connecting an external source. We configure the program to receive 500 results per second. Each time the ADS1291 reports that a measurement is complete, the microcontroller reads the service data and the 24-bit voltage value.

The program combines the received bits into a signed number. To express it in volts, we need to account for the ADC reference voltage and the configured gain. We compare the sequence of values obtained with the characteristics of the internal test signal. If the changes repeat as expected, this means that the measurement IC and digital communication are working together.

However, the built-in test signal does not pass through the external measurement contacts. It therefore does not allow us to test the entire electronic system we have created.

We now use the ECG simulator that we discussed earlier. After checking that its electrical outputs are compatible with our board's inputs, we connect the simulator in place of the electrodes. We set a known signal and obtain a sequence of measurements. For example, at a sampling rate of 500 Hz, about 5000 samples should arrive in 10 seconds. We check their number, the regularity of their arrival, and whether the measured voltage changes match the specified signal.

Thus, we move from separate electronic components to a system capable of obtaining digital data on changes in electrical voltage. But a sequence of numbers is still inconvenient for studying the heart's activity. We need to display it as a cardiogram and learn to detect signal distortions.
content_json.title: Testing the measurement system on a laboratory test bench
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Texas Instruments — ADS1291, ADS1292, ADS1292R Datasheet.
sources.quote: Section 8.3.2.2 describes the built-in test signal generator, which allows the chip's measurement circuitry to be checked. Sections 8.5 and 8.6 cover the transfer of results via SPI and register configuration. Used when developing a program for laboratory testing of the measurement channel.

stickers.text:
The card describes the laboratory test procedure, but does not confirm that the tests have already been performed. Practical testing requires a manufactured and checked electronic board, a data acquisition program, and a compatible ECG simulator.

The ADS1291 built-in test signal does not test the board's external measurement inputs or protection circuits. Testing with a simulator allows this part of the system to be investigated, but does not in itself confirm the device's medical accuracy or safety.

Until the necessary checks have been completed, the experimental electrocardiograph must not be connected to a person.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: testing the ADS1291
stickers.text:
We begin laboratory testing after manufacturing and checking the electronic board. At this stage, we use only the ADS1291 internal test signals and laboratory equipment. Connecting a person is ruled out.

First, under the teacher's supervision, we check the power supply. The ADS1291 analog section must receive the 3.0 V specified by our circuit, and the digital section must receive 3.3 V. If the voltages differ from the design values or a fault is detected, we stop the test.

After that, we check communication between the ADS1291 and ESP32-S3. We load the prepared program, send the SDATAC command, and read the ID register. For the ADS1291, the two least significant bits of this register must have the value 10 in binary. We check the remaining bits against the documentation. If the IC responds incorrectly, we check the power supply, clocking, and SPI connections.

We then write the hexadecimal value 02 to the CONFIG1 register. With the specified clocking, it corresponds to a rate of 500 samples per second. We enable the internal 2.42 V reference voltage through the CONFIG2 register and check that the settings have been written correctly.

We perform the first measurement without an external signal. To do this, we set the value 01 in the CH1SET register. It connects the measurement inputs inside the ADS1291. We obtain a sequence of digital values and observe their changes. Since the voltage difference at the connected inputs should be close to zero, the results should be near some constant level. Small deviations may arise from the measurement system's own noise and offset.

The next test is to record the internal test signal. To do this, we write the value A3 to the CONFIG2 register and the value 05 to CH1SET. These settings enable the internal 1 Hz square-wave generator and route it to the measurement channel. The gain remains at 6 times.

With an internal reference voltage of 2.42 V, the test signal amplitude at the amplifier input is approximately 1.008 mV. One complete period lasts about one second. At a sampling rate of 500 Hz, approximately 500 measurement results should appear during this period.

The microcontroller receives each result after the DRDY signal appears. For the ADS1291, we read six bytes: three bytes of information about the IC's status and three bytes containing the measurement result for the first channel.

The program combines the last three bytes into a signed 24-bit number. It then converts it to millivolts, accounting for the reference voltage and gain. The graph should show periodic changes between two voltage levels. The transitions may be smoothed by the ADC's internal digital filtering.

To check continuous recording, we obtain 5000 consecutive samples. At a nominal rate of 500 Hz, this corresponds to approximately ten seconds. We check that the data arrive in the correct order and that the program does not lose measurement results.

Only after successfully testing the internal signal do we move on to the external ECG simulator. Connecting it requires a preliminary compatibility check with our board's measurement inputs. Unlike the internal test, this will allow us to investigate the signal's passage through the external connections and input circuits.

stickers.title: Sample laboratory test report
stickers.text:
Laboratory test report for the measurement system

Equipment used: ADS1291 board, ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1, laboratory measuring instruments.

Power supply check: actual measured voltages of the analog and digital sections—enter the values obtained.

SPI check: ID register value—enter the number read. Compliance with the documentation—confirm or describe the deviation detected.

Sampling rate: configured value—500 Hz. Actual number of samples received and recording duration—enter based on the test results.

Internal input connection test: average voltage value—enter. Spread of results relative to the average—enter.

Internal test signal check: configured frequency—1 Hz. Expected amplitude—approximately 1.008 mV. Measured frequency and amplitude—enter.

Data integrity check: number of missed samples—enter.

Detected deviations, possible causes, and necessary corrections—describe.

Final conclusion: which functions were tested successfully, which do not work, and which tests still need to be performed.

content_json.html:
In card No. 19, we determined how the measurement system should obtain a sequence of numbers corresponding to changes in electrical voltage. However, the numbers alone do not yet allow us to observe the heart's activity visually. To do this, we need to show how the voltage changes over time.

Each ADS1291 result is a signed 24-bit number. To determine the voltage it corresponds to, the program takes into account the ADC reference voltage and the gain of the measurement circuit. We convert the resulting value to millivolts.

Now each measurement needs to be associated with a point in time. At a sampling rate of 500 Hz, a new value appears every 2 milliseconds. We can therefore use the sample's sequence number to determine how much time has elapsed since the start of the recording. For example, sample number 250, if numbering starts at zero, corresponds to a time of 0.5 seconds.

To plot the graph, we will transfer the results from the ESP32-S3 to a computer via USB. The microcontroller program places the acquired values and their sequence numbers in a temporary memory area—a buffer. The data is transferred from this buffer to the computer. A separate program on the computer receives the data and plots the points in sequence.

We plot time in seconds on the horizontal axis and voltage in millivolts on the vertical axis. We connect neighboring points with lines to obtain a visual representation of changes in the electrical signal. If the simulator reproduces a characteristic ECG waveform, the corresponding waves should appear on the graph.

To observe the changes continuously, the program updates the graph as new measurements arrive. For example, we can display the last 10 seconds of the signal, or about 5000 samples at the selected sampling rate.

The numerical measurement results now become a visual cardiogram whose shape can be compared with the simulator's signal. However, the graph may contain not only the useful signal but also unwanted voltage changes, and individual samples may be lost during data transfer. Therefore, we need to learn to distinguish genuine ECG changes from distortions arising during measurement.
content_json.title: Plotting a cardiogram from measurement results
content_json.author: ai_checked
