stickers.text:
Plotting a graph does not yet mean that an ECG display program has been created. Implementation requires separately writing a data transfer program for the ESP32-S3 and a program to receive and display the data on the computer.

In addition, connecting points with lines merely provides a visual representation of individual measurements: it does not reconstruct all the voltage changes between them exactly. It is also necessary to check that data arrives without missing samples and that each sample corresponds to the correct point in time.

Connecting the laboratory system to a computer via USB does not confirm that it is safe for a person. Testing continues to be performed only with artificial signals.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: from an ADC number to a point on the graph
stickers.text:
Let us use a specific example to see how an ADS1291 result becomes a point on a cardiogram.

Suppose the ADC reference voltage is 2.42 V and the gain is set to 6.

For each measurement, the ADS1291 sends the microcontroller three bytes of auxiliary data and three bytes containing the measurement result. The last three bytes are combined into a signed 24-bit number.

Suppose the program has received three consecutive results: 2080, 12480, and 2080. They have been assigned sample numbers 100, 101, and 102.

First, we determine the time of each measurement. At a sampling rate of 500 Hz, we obtain:

Sample No. 100—0.200 seconds.

Sample No. 101—0.202 seconds.

Sample No. 102—0.204 seconds.

Now we convert the digital values to voltage. For an ideal ADC, we use the following relationship: the measured voltage equals the digital value multiplied by the reference voltage and divided by the product of the gain and the number 8 388 607.

With the selected settings, we obtain approximately the following values:

2080 corresponds to 0.10 mV.

12480 corresponds to 0.60 mV.

2080 corresponds to 0.10 mV.

Now we mark three points on the graph: the first corresponds to a time of 0.200 seconds and a voltage of 0.10 mV, the second to 0.202 seconds and 0.60 mV, and the third to 0.204 seconds and 0.10 mV.

By connecting neighboring points with lines, we obtain a segment of the graph. The remaining points of the cardiogram are plotted in the same way.

This is a simplified numerical example, not the results of an actual measurement. In an operational program, it is also necessary to handle negative digital values correctly and take the actual ADC settings into account.

content_json.html:
We have learned to represent measurement results as a cardiogram. However, the resulting graph does not necessarily reproduce the original electrical signal accurately. To identify the causes of possible distortions, we compare our device's recording with the signal produced by the ECG simulator.

Since we know the characteristics of the artificial signal, we can detect differences between the expected cardiogram and the one obtained. For example, additional voltage fluctuations that were not present in the original signal may appear on the graph.

These fluctuations arise because the measurement system picks up more than just the useful signal. The electric field of the power supply network can affect the connecting wires and cause interference at a frequency of 50 Hz. The device's electronic components also produce small random voltage changes, called noise.

When measuring a person's ECG, other sources of distortion also arise. Changes in the contact between the electrodes and the skin, for example during movement, can cause the entire cardiogram to shift slowly upward or downward. This is called baseline drift. In addition, the electrical activity of other muscles can be superimposed on the heart's signal and create additional fluctuations.

In our laboratory system, we can investigate electrical interference and noise by comparing the simulator's known signal with the measurement results. However, the appearance of the graph alone does not always allow us to determine the cause of a distortion: additional checks are needed.

It turns out that simply measuring voltage is not enough. We must preserve the changes associated with the heart's activity and, where possible, exclude unwanted influences. Moreover, eliminating interference must not lead to the loss of useful information.

Therefore, we need to understand how to separate useful ECG changes from interference and which signal processing methods allow us to do this.
content_json.title: Finding out where ECG distortions come from
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Texas Instruments — Smart Sensing with Ultra-low-power MCUs – Part 4: Holter Monitor.
sources.quote: A technical article by a manufacturer of measurement chips. Explains the effects of electromagnetic interference, the 50/60 Hz mains frequency, baseline drift, electrode movement, and muscle activity on ECG quality. Discusses the need for filtering while preserving the diagnostically significant signal shape.

stickers.text:
A typical ECG simulator reproduces an artificial electrical signal, but does not necessarily simulate electrode movement, changes in skin contact, or muscle interference.

Therefore, comparing the recording with the simulator's signal allows the measurement system to be checked, but does not reproduce all the conditions of recording an ECG from a person. Additional laboratory tests will be needed to check resistance to specific types of interference.

It is also important to distinguish between distortion of the measured voltage and loss of digital samples during data transfer: these are different faults requiring different methods of detection and correction.

content_json.html:
We have found that the measured ECG signal may contain unwanted voltage fluctuations. To bring the resulting cardiogram closer to the original signal, we need to reduce the influence of interference while preserving the electrical changes associated with the heart's activity.

We use digital filtering for this purpose. It involves processing the sequence of numbers obtained from the ADC. The program compares neighboring values and changes them according to specific mathematical rules. As a result, some signal changes are attenuated more strongly than others.

Different types of interference require different processing. Slow baseline shifts can be reduced by determining the gradually changing signal level and subtracting it from the measured values. This method allows slow voltage changes to be attenuated while preserving faster ones. High-pass filters perform this task.

Interference from the power grid is distinctive because it produces fluctuations at a specific frequency—usually 50 or 60 Hz. To attenuate these particular fluctuations, we use a notch filter. It reduces signal components within a narrow frequency range, leaving the others relatively unchanged.

To attenuate rapid fluctuations, including some muscle interference, we use a low-pass filter. It reduces abrupt changes between neighboring values. For example, this can be done by calculating the average of several consecutive samples. But along with the interference, this type of filter can also smooth out rapid changes in the actual ECG signal.

It turns out that filtering does not simply remove interference; it changes the measured data. The more strongly we suppress particular fluctuations, the greater the likelihood of also changing useful information if it contains the same frequencies.

We therefore provide options in the program to enable and disable the filters and to change their parameters. We save the original measurement results separately from the processed results. By comparing both versions with the simulator's known signal, we check which types of interference have been reduced and how much the cardiogram's shape itself has changed.

We can now not only display the electrical signal but also control its processing. However, even a well-filtered cardiogram is not necessarily reliable: for example, poor electrode contact or a fault in the measurement system can lead to incorrect results. We therefore need to check not only the signal's shape but also the conditions under which it was acquired.
content_json.title: Reducing ECG distortions through filtering
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Texas Instruments — Smart Sensing with Ultra-low-power MCUs, Part 4: Holter Monitor.
sources.quote: An official technical article on ECG recording. Explains the effects of baseline drift and 50/60 Hz mains interference, and the need to select filtering parameters with signal shape preservation in mind. The section on ECG processing for clinical interpretation is particularly useful.

stickers.text:
The principle of digital filtering is explained here, but the specific algorithms, their software implementation, and their parameters have not yet been defined. Practical application requires selecting filters, implementing them, and checking the results using known signals.

Filtering cannot restore information that was lost during measurement, for example because of ADC overload. It can also distort diagnostically significant portions of the ECG. The original recording must therefore be saved, and the quality of the processed signal must be checked separately.

Successful filtering of an artificial signal does not yet confirm that the device is suitable for medical diagnosis.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: how the program filters numbers
stickers.text:
Let us consider the simplest digital filter using three consecutive values obtained in the previous example: 0.10 mV, 0.60 mV, and 0.10 mV.

Suppose the abrupt voltage change to 0.60 mV was caused by interference. We want to reduce its influence on the graph.

To do this, we can replace the value at the middle point with the arithmetic mean of three neighboring samples.

We add the values: 0.10 + 0.60 + 0.10 = 0.80 mV.

We divide the sum by the number of samples: 0.80 / 3 ≈ 0.27 mV.

Thus, instead of the original value of 0.60 mV, after processing we obtain approximately 0.27 mV.

If we repeat these calculations for all points, gradually moving the group of three samples along the recording, the graph will become smoother. This method is called a moving average.

However, a problem arises. If the change to 0.60 mV was not interference but part of the actual ECG signal, the filter will still reduce it. Therefore, the filter does not recognize the cause of the voltage change; it only performs the specified mathematical operations.

In addition, averaging three neighboring samples is not a complete method for eliminating 50 Hz mains interference, baseline drift, or muscle interference. For each task, an appropriate filter must be selected and its effect on the useful signal checked.

The program must therefore be tested on a recording with a known ECG waveform. We save the original values and compare the filtering results with them. This allows us to establish which changes were reduced and which features of the original signal were distorted.

content_json.html:
We have learned to measure an electrical signal, convert it into numbers, and reduce the effects of interference. However, even a correctly recorded cardiogram does not mean that the device is safe for a person. Measuring an ECG requires an electrical connection to the body, but this very connection can become a source of danger if the device malfunctions.

We must therefore modify the design of the measurement system so that it not only receives the heart's weak signal but also prevents dangerous electric current from passing through the human body.

This primarily concerns the inputs to which the electrodes are connected. We provide protective electrical circuits between the electrodes and the ADS1291. Their task is to limit possible currents and voltages during faults without interfering with normal measurement of the weak ECG signal. Protective components must therefore be selected with both electrical safety and measurement accuracy in mind.

But dangerous voltage can enter through more than just the measurement inputs. Our device receives power and exchanges data with other electronic devices. For example, connecting to a computer via USB creates an additional electrical connection through which, under certain fault conditions, a dangerous current path may arise.

To prevent this, medical measurement systems use electrical isolation between the parts connected to the person and external equipment. One method is galvanic isolation. It allows information to be transmitted between devices without a direct electrical connection between their conductors.

Using a rechargeable battery instead of a permanent connection to a mains-powered supply reduces the device's dependence on external power, but does not in itself guarantee safety. Both charging mode and possible faults in electronic components must be considered.

In addition, according to the technical specification, the device must be protected against the effects of a defibrillator. Its electrical pulse can damage sensitive measurement inputs. A medical design therefore requires special protection against such effects.

Thus, ensuring safety directly changes the electrocardiograph we are creating. It is no longer enough to connect the electrodes to the measurement IC: we need to develop a protected measurement input, a safe power system, and a safe system for electrical interaction with external devices.

However, protective circuits also affect the passage of the weak ECG signal. We therefore need to determine which characteristics of the measurement system allow it to maintain measurement reliability while meeting safety requirements.
content_json.title: Protecting the person and the electronic system
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: IEC 60601-1:2005+AMD1:2012+AMD2:2020 — Medical electrical equipment. General requirements for basic safety and essential performance.
sources.quote: The official page for the international standard IEC 60601-1. The standard establishes general requirements for the basic safety and essential performance of medical electrical equipment, including protection against electrical hazards. The full text of the standard is distributed separately.

sources.title: Texas Instruments — ADS1291, ADS1292, ADS1292R Datasheet.
sources.quote: Official ADS1291 documentation. Section 8.3.10.2 discusses electrodes and their monitoring; the manufacturer specifically states the need to comply with permissible currents through the patient. The application examples also note that the circuits for protecting the patient and the measurement inputs are not shown in the circuit diagram provided.

stickers.text:
This card establishes the need for electrical protection, but the protective system itself has not yet been developed.

Practical implementation requires a circuit diagram of the protective circuits, calculation of their parameters, identification of the required isolation barriers, and professional testing for compliance with applicable medical standards. Protection against the external electrical effects specified in the technical specification will also need to be confirmed separately.

Neither the presence of an ADS1291, nor battery power, nor individual protective components in themselves make the device safe to connect to a person.

The student design described here therefore remains a laboratory prototype intended for testing with artificial electrical signals.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: how protection changes the measurement sys
stickers.text:
Let us consider how safety requirements change the design of our electrocardiograph.

If we only needed to measure voltage, we could consider connecting the signal source directly to the ADS1291 measurement inputs. However, the future medical device must interact with a person, and dangerous voltages and currents may arise if its electronic components malfunction.

A protective section must therefore be provided between the external contacts and the measurement IC. Its task is to limit dangerous electrical effects without interfering with measurement of the weak signal.

A new problem arises here. Protective components also have electrical properties: resistance, capacitance, and possible leakage currents. They can therefore affect the voltage passing through them. If the properties of the protective circuits for the two measurement inputs differ, identical interference at these inputs can turn into an additional measured voltage difference.

Thus, protection cannot be developed separately from the measurement system and then simply added to a finished board. Its electrical properties must be taken into account when designing and testing the entire measurement channel.

A similar problem arises when connecting external equipment. USB connects our device to a computer, which may have its own power supply and electrical connections. We therefore need to determine which parts of the device must be electrically isolated from one another and under what conditions an external connection is permitted.

As a result, ensuring safety changes not only the number of components but also the organization of the electrical system itself. Each protective solution must be tested both for its ability to prevent dangerous effects and for its ability to maintain measurement reliability.

content_json.html:
We have provided protection for the person against dangerous electrical effects and learned to reduce interference on the cardiogram. However, protective components and the measurement circuit itself can affect the electrical signal. We therefore need to check how accurately the device measures voltage and whether it can detect conditions under which the results become unreliable.

First, let us consider the interaction between the measurement device and the signal source. When we connect electrodes to the measurement inputs, a small current may flow through them. If the measurement device draws too much current, this causes an additional voltage drop across the resistance of the electrodes and skin. As a result, the measured potential difference may differ from the original one. To reduce this effect, the measurement circuit must have high input impedance.

Another problem involves interference that affects both measurement inputs simultaneously. For example, the electric field of the power mains may cause nearly identical voltage changes at each input. Such effects are called common-mode interference. Since we measure the voltage difference, ideally the identical component should cancel out through subtraction. However, in a real circuit this does not happen completely. The measurement system's ability to reject such interference is characterized by the CMRR ratio: the higher it is, the less common-mode interference affects the result.

Even in the absence of external interference, electronic components generate their own electrical noise. To investigate it, we use a laboratory source with a constant, known voltage difference. If the device's readings continue to vary randomly, these fluctuations allow us to assess the noise of the measurement system. Its magnitude must be compared with the permissible level established for the future device.

However, reliability depends on more than the characteristics of the electronics. If an electrode loses contact with the skin, the electrical signal may no longer reach the device's input correctly. The ADS1291 contains a special electrode lead-off detection system. It generates a small electrical monitoring signal and determines the state of the connection from the response. The test result is available to the microcontroller program. On the laboratory test bench, we can investigate this function by simulating an intact connection and its interruption.

We now need to combine the test results. The program must take into account the state of the connections, the presence of excessive noise, measured voltage outside the permissible range, and loss of digital samples. If a problem is detected, the device reports that the signal quality is insufficient for reliable processing.

Thus, we are creating not just a measurement system, but a device capable of detecting some causes of unreliability in its own results. Only after checking the quality of the resulting recording does it make sense to use it to determine heart rate (HR).
content_json.title: Checking the reliability of electrical measurement
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Texas Instruments — ADS1291, ADS1292, ADS1292R Datasheet (Rev. C).
sources.quote: Section 6.5 contains the characteristics of input impedance, noise level, and common-mode rejection (CMRR). Section 8.3.10.2 explains electrode lead-off detection, and section 8.6.1.9 explains how to obtain information about electrode status through the LOFF_STAT register.

sources.title: Texas Instruments — Understanding Lead-Off Detection in ECG (Rev. A).
sources.quote: The technical guide explains how changes in electrical contact affect ECG measurement and how electrode disconnection is detected using a DC or AC monitoring signal. It discusses the limitations of these methods.

stickers.text:
The technical specification lists input impedance, CMRR, and noise level, but does not establish specific permissible values for them. These characteristics must therefore be defined before acceptance testing.

The ADS1291 parameters provided by the manufacturer apply to the IC itself and to specific operating conditions. They do not guarantee that the assembled electrocardiograph will have the same characteristics: the result is affected by protective circuits, connecting conductors, the power supply, and board design.

It is also important to distinguish between detecting poor contact and confirming safety. The electrode monitoring system helps identify some measurement problems, but does not prove the device's electrical safety. For now, its operation is intended to be tested only on a laboratory simulator.

Finally, developing a software quality indicator does not yet mean that it can detect all possible ECG distortions. This requires separate criteria and tests.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: how to test input impedance,
stickers.text:
To understand why the characteristics of the measurement circuit affect ECG reliability, let us consider three situations on the laboratory test bench.

The first situation concerns input impedance.

Suppose the laboratory source produces a voltage difference of 1 mV. When the measurement device is connected, some current may pass through its inputs. If the input impedance is not high enough, this changes the voltage we want to measure.

For testing, a source with known electrical characteristics is used, and the measured voltage is compared under different connection conditions. If the readings change, we need to determine the role played by the resistance of the source and of the measurement system itself.

The second situation concerns common-mode interference.

Suppose the voltage at the first input relative to a common point is 1.001 V, and at the second it is 1.000 V. The difference between them is 0.001 V, or 1 mV.

Now imagine that external interference simultaneously increases both voltages by 0.050 V. We obtain 1.051 V and 1.050 V. The difference is still 1 mV.

An ideal differential measurement should preserve the original result. If identical interference changes the measured difference, this means that the measurement system does not fully reject the common-mode effect. CMRR characterizes the ability to perform this rejection.

The third situation concerns intrinsic noise.

Suppose the source produces a constant voltage difference, but the device displays slightly different values in succession. To assess these fluctuations, we calculate the mean value and examine the deviations of individual measurements from it.

However, not every fluctuation is caused by the IC itself. The result is also affected by the signal source, power supply, connecting conductors, and external interference. We therefore need to distinguish between measuring the ADC's own noise and measuring the noise of the entire electronic system.

Finally, we repeat the tests with the electrode lead-off detection system enabled. It applies an additional electrical stimulus to the inputs, so it may change the measurement conditions and cause an additional shift in the result.

Thus, we test not only the individual characteristics of the IC, but also how they change when measurement, contact monitoring, and protective components operate together.

content_json.html:
We have learned to obtain an ECG trace and identify some causes of unreliable measurements. Now we need to extract information about how the heart works from it. We will begin by determining heart rate (HR)—the number of heart contractions in one minute.

On the ECG trace, the electrical processes associated with each cardiac cycle form a characteristic sequence of waves. One part of this sequence is called the QRS complex. It reflects the spread of electrical excitation through the heart's ventricles, followed by their contraction. A prominent R wave can usually be identified within this complex.

To determine HR, the program must find successive QRS complexes and establish when they occur. To do this, it can analyze how quickly the voltage changes and identify sections with characteristic sharp deflections. After detecting such a section, the program marks the position of the R wave and checks whether the detected change is interference or part of a complex already detected.

Now we can measure the time between two successive R waves. This time span is called the R–R interval. It allows us to determine how frequently cardiac cycles recur.

For example, at a sampling rate of 500 Hz, the program detected two successive R waves at sample numbers 1000 and 1400. There were 400 samples between them, which is 400 / 500 = 0.8 seconds. To find the number of such cycles per minute, we divide 60 seconds by 0.8 seconds. We obtain an HR of 75 beats per minute.

If the durations of adjacent intervals differ, the program can calculate the average HR over several cycles. However, a single average number does not show how regularly the heart is working. It is therefore important to save the intervals between the detected complexes as well.

For testing, we use an ECG simulator. We set, for example, 60 and 90 cardiac cycles per minute, obtain recordings, and compare the HR calculated by the program with the set values. If there are errors in QRS complex detection or the signal quality is insufficient, the program must not present the result as reliable.

Thus, we turn a sequence of voltage measurements into a quantitative characteristic of cardiac activity. Now we need to save the resulting ECG trace together with the calculated HR so that the study results can be examined later.
content_json.title: Determining heart rate (HR)
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: RR Intervals, Heart Rate, and HRV Howto — George B. Moody, PhysioNet.
sources.quote: The PhysioNet tutorial explains how to determine R–R intervals from an electrocardiogram, select characteristic points of the QRS complex, and calculate heart rate. It includes examples of processing ECG recordings in software.

stickers.text:
The card describes the principle of calculating HR, but a complete algorithm for detecting QRS complexes has not yet been implemented or tested.

Simply detecting sharp voltage changes may incorrectly identify interference or other ECG waves as QRS complexes. Unusual signal shapes and rhythm disturbances make the task more difficult. Reliable operation will require selecting a QRS detection algorithm and testing it on annotated ECG recordings with various characteristics.

An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart, not mechanical contractions directly. Therefore, the HR calculated from it characterizes the frequency of detected electrical cardiac cycles and does not replace a medical assessment of heart function.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: how the program detects complexes
stickers.text:
To calculate HR, the program must first determine where one cardiac cycle ends and the next begins on the ECG trace.

To do this, it examines the ECG samples in sequence and looks for sections characteristic of the QRS complex. In particular, the program can evaluate the rate of voltage change, the magnitude of the deflection, and the duration of the detected change.

However, a single large deflection does not yet mean that a QRS complex has been found. It may be caused by interference. The program therefore needs additional conditions that allow it to distinguish characteristic ECG changes from unrelated fluctuations and avoid treating different sections of one complex as several cardiac cycles.

After detecting a complex, the program determines its position in time and saves the corresponding sample number.

Suppose the program detected four successive QRS complexes at sample numbers 300, 700, 1100, and 1500. At a sampling rate of 500 Hz, there are 400 samples, or 0.8 seconds, between adjacent complexes.

We obtain three intervals of 0.8 seconds each. Therefore, the recurrence rate of the detected cardiac cycles is 60 / 0.8 = 75 per minute.

To test the algorithm, we use an artificial ECG trace with known QRS complex positions. We compare the positions found by the program with the expected ones. We separately record missed complexes and cases where interference was incorrectly identified as a cardiac cycle.

If the program cannot confidently identify QRS complexes, it must mark the result as unreliable rather than output an arbitrary HR value.

The method described illustrates the principle of detecting cardiac cycles, but it is not yet a complete and tested algorithm. For practical implementation, a specific QRS detector must be selected and its performance investigated using recordings with different signal shapes and interference.

content_json.html:
We have learned to plot an ECG trace and determine heart rate from it. However, until now, the results have been sent to a computer for real-time observation. If the program stops running and the data remain only in RAM, the resulting ECG trace will disappear.

To allow the study to be examined again, we need to save not only an image of the graph but also the sequence of measured voltage values together with information about the conditions under which they were obtained.

According to the technical specification, we provide for a recording lasting from 10 to 30 seconds. At a sampling rate of 500 Hz, we obtain 5000 samples in 10 seconds and 15 000 in 30 seconds. These values form the basis of the saved recording.

For the initial laboratory device, we use the computer with which the ESP32-S3 already exchanges data via USB. The microcontroller assigns each sample a sequential number and transmits the data in small batches. The computer program receives them, temporarily places them in a buffer, and writes them to a file on disk. Unlike RAM, data on disk are retained after the program stops running.

But voltage values alone are not enough. For example, a sequence of 5000 numbers cannot be correctly reconstructed in time if the sampling rate is unknown. Therefore, along with the results, we save the measurement rate, the lead used, the gain settings, and information about the filters applied.

To distinguish one study from another, we assign each a unique identifier. The computer program also saves the recording's start date and time, its duration, and the calculated HR. Future medical use will require patient identification. While we are working with an ECG simulator, we use a training test designation instead of actual patient data.

Before finishing the recording, we check the number of samples received and the sequence of their numbers. If some data have been lost, the program marks the recording as incomplete. We save the original measurements separately from the filtering results so that processing can be repeated if necessary.

Thus, the ECG trace changes from a temporarily displayed graph into a saved study that can be reopened and checked. However, we now need to decide how to present this recording as a human-readable report and files suitable for exchange with other programs.
content_json.title: Saving the study results
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Espressif — USB Serial/JTAG Controller Console, ESP32-S3.
sources.quote: Official documentation for the ESP32-S3's built-in USB Serial/JTAG controller. It explains the capability for bidirectional serial data exchange between the microcontroller and a computer. It is used as the basis for transmitting ECG results in the laboratory.

sources.title: Espressif — File System Considerations, ESP32-S3.
sources.quote: The official guide to choosing a file system for saving data in the ESP32-S3's flash memory. It will be needed at the next stage if the portable device must save studies without a connected computer.

stickers.text:
We have defined the contents of the saved recording and the principle of data transmission, but the saving mechanism itself has not yet been implemented or tested.

In the laboratory version, the file is created on the computer. If USB is disconnected or the receiving program is closed during measurement, the recording may be incomplete. A portable device capable of operating without a computer will require a separate arrangement for storing data in nonvolatile memory and testing its reliability.

In addition, saving a patient identifier and medical data will require measures to protect confidential information. Only artificial signals and fictitious identifiers are used in the training tests.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: how to check recording completeness
stickers.text:
Let us consider saving one ten-second ECG recording at a sampling rate of 500 Hz.

During the recording, the ADS1291 should obtain 5000 measurement results. Each result contains 24 bits, or three bytes. Therefore, the numerical voltage values alone will occupy 15 000 bytes, not including sample numbers and the remaining study information.

When the microcontroller receives a new value, the program assigns it a sequential number. Several successive values are then combined into a batch of data that is transmitted to the computer.

For example, the first batch may contain sample numbers 0 to 99, and the second, 100 to 199. As the data arrive, the computer program saves them to disk.

After receiving each new batch, the program checks whether the sequence of numbers continues without gaps. If sample No. 201 arrives after sample No. 199, sample No. 200 is missing. The program must record the gap rather than silently connect adjacent points on the graph.

However, numbering detects only losses that occur after a number has been assigned. If the microcontroller failed to receive a result from the ADS1291 at all, missed measurement-ready events and possible buffer overflow must also be monitored.

At the end of the recording, the program checks the number and sequence of samples against the expected values. If all data have been received, the file can be marked as a complete recording. If data losses, a connection interruption, or a saving error are detected, the study must remain marked as incomplete.

Along with the samples, we save the sampling rate, measurement settings, study identifier, and information about the problems identified.

Thus, we save not just a sequence of numbers but a recording whose completeness can be checked. This is necessary so that a subsequent program does not treat an incomplete ECG trace as a reliable study.

content_json.html:
We have learned to save an ECG trace together with study information. However, a saved sequence of numbers is not yet convenient to send to another person or use in another program. To make the results available for examination and transmission, we need to present them in commonly accepted file formats.

First, we create a CSV file. It is a text table in which values are separated by a particular character, such as a comma. The program writes rows in sequence: the sample number, the time it was obtained, and the measured voltage in millivolts. If filtering was applied, the processed value can be saved in a separate column. Such a file can be opened in a spreadsheet or used for further calculations.

However, an ECG study requires not only the measurements themselves but also information about the conditions under which they were obtained. We therefore create an XML file. In it, information is organized using named elements. For example, information about the lead, sampling rate, recording duration, samples obtained, HR, and signal quality can be placed inside an element representing the study. This structure allows a program to distinguish the purpose of individual data items rather than determine it solely from the arrangement of columns.

But examining thousands of numbers or an XML structure is inconvenient for a physician. The physician needs to see the ECG trace and the main study results. We therefore also create a report in PDF format.

To do this, the program reads the saved data, plots a graph with time and voltage labels, and places it on a page together with the study identifier, date, recording duration, lead name, calculated HR, and signal quality assessment. We separately indicate the filters applied and any possible recording problems. For a laboratory study, we must note that the signal was obtained from an ECG simulator.

Thus, from one saved recording, we obtain three different representations: CSV for working with numerical measurements, XML for structured data exchange, and PDF for human viewing of the results. All three files must be generated from the same original recording so that the values and study information do not contradict one another.

After creating the files, we check that they open, contain the correct number of samples, and retain the necessary information. The study results can now be not only observed and stored but also transmitted to other people and information systems. We therefore need to arrange for their transmission to a physician.
content_json.title: Creating an ECG report and files
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Python Documentation — csv: CSV File Reading and Writing.
sources.quote: Official documentation on creating CSV files, writing column names, and saving rows containing measurement results. It is used to export digital ECG samples.

sources.title: W3C — Extensible Markup Language (XML) 1.0 (Fifth Edition).
sources.quote: The official XML specification. It describes the rules for structuring data using named elements and attributes. It is used to represent ECG results and study information.

sources.title: ReportLab — User Guide, Chapter 2: Graphics and Text with pdfgen.
sources.quote: The official guide to creating PDF documents programmatically. It explains how to place text, lines, and graphical elements on pages. It can be used to generate a report containing an ECG trace.

stickers.text:
The card explains the purpose of the three formats and the principle of creating the files, but their software implementation has not yet been completed.

For CSV and XML, the exact structure of the saved data must be defined, including units of measurement, time information, and the notation for missing samples. For PDF, a report template will need to be developed and the ECG trace checked for correct display.

An ordinary XML file created using a custom structure does not automatically become compatible with medical information systems. Such exchange may require specialized standards, such as SCP-ECG or DICOM, which we will consider separately.

The presence of a PDF report also does not mean that the resulting ECG trace has undergone medical interpretation or is suitable for making a diagnosis.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: three files from one study
stickers.text:
Let us take one saved artificial ECG recording lasting 10 seconds. Its identifier is TEST-001, its sampling rate is 500 Hz, its sample count is 5000, and its lead is I.

Suppose the first three measured voltage values are 0.10 mV, 0.12 mV, and 0.09 mV. These are hypothetical values chosen solely to explain the structure of the files.

First, we create CSV. The program writes the column names: study identifier, sampling rate, sample number, time, and voltage.

The first data row will contain TEST-001, 500, 0, 0.000, 0.10.

The second: TEST-001, 500, 1, 0.002, 0.12.

The third: TEST-001, 500, 2, 0.004, 0.09.

All 5000 samples are written in sequence in this way. CSV allows another program to read the data as a table.

Now we create XML. Unlike CSV, here we can organize the data by meaning. Inside the study element, we place separate elements containing the identifier TEST-001, the lead name, the sampling rate, the signal source, and the measurement results.

We also save information about recording quality, detected gaps, filter settings, and the calculated HR. The program reading the XML must understand the structure of these elements that we have agreed upon.

Finally, we create PDF. The program plots a graph from the same 5000 samples and places it in the report. Alongside it, we indicate the identifier TEST-001, recording parameters, HR, and signal quality information. We must note that the study was performed using an ECG simulator.

The three files thus represent the same recording in different ways. Therefore, when creating each file, the program must use the same original data.

For verification, we reopen the CSV and XML files, reconstruct the measurement sequence from them, and compare it with the original recording. In the PDF, we check the correctness of the graph, the time and amplitude scales, and the study information.

In this way, we confirm that changing how the data are represented has not led to an unnoticed loss or substitution of medical information.

content_json.title: Creating a portable electrocardiograph and transmitting medical data

content_json.html:
We have learned to save study results and present them in PDF, CSV and XML formats. However, for medical use, simply obtaining a file containing a cardiogram is not enough. We need to make it possible to send the results to a physician who can review them regardless of where the measurement was performed.

In the laboratory system, we already use USB to transfer data from the ESP32-S3 to a computer. But if the electrocardiograph is to operate as a standalone portable device, a permanent connection to a computer becomes inconvenient. We therefore need to arrange wireless data transmission.

The ESP32-S3 microcontroller we selected supports Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) and Wi-Fi. Using BLE, the device can establish a connection, for example with a smartphone, and send data to it in small batches. The smartphone application receives these batches and combines them into an ECG recording. The smartphone can then send the study over the internet to a remote server.

Another approach is to use Wi-Fi. In this case, the microcontroller connects to a wireless network and sends the results to the server on its own. For this transmission, the program must know the server address and the rules for exchanging data with it.

However, transmitting information does not yet mean delivering it correctly. Therefore, along with the cardiogram, we send the study identifier, information about the recording time, sampling rate, lead, signal quality and calculated heart rate (HR). The receiving program checks that the data are complete. If the connection is interrupted, transmission must resume without any part of the study being lost unnoticed.

After receiving the data, the server saves the study and links it to the corresponding patient identifier. The physician accesses the recording through a medical information system (MIS), and the study results can be included in an electronic medical record (EMR).

Application programming interfaces — API — are used to allow different programs to exchange information about the study. They define which requests can be sent to the system, which data must be transmitted and which responses it returns.

But an API alone is not enough for compatibility with medical systems. The structure of the data themselves must also be agreed upon. For example, standardized formats such as SCP-ECG and DICOM exist for exchanging ECG data. They establish rules for representing the electrical signal and the associated medical information. An ordinary XML file from the previous card does not automatically become compatible with these standards.

Since medical information is confidential data, we need to restrict who can receive it and protect transmission against unauthorized access. For exchanges with the server, we provide for a secure connection, authentication of the participants and access permissions.

Thus, the electrocardiograph we have created gains the ability to send study results for remote review by a physician. Software analysis, including the use of AI, may also be applied in the future, but its reliability must be confirmed separately.

To use the device outside the laboratory, one more task now remains: enabling it to operate independently without a permanent connection to a computer or an external power source.
content_json.title: Transmitting the study results to a physician
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Bluetooth® Low Energy - ESP32-S3 - — ESP-IDF Programming Guide v6.1 documentation
sources.quote: Official Espressif documentation on Bluetooth Low Energy. Explains device discovery, connection and data exchange through GATT services and characteristics. Used to develop ECG transmission between the ESP32-S3 and a smartphone.

sources.title: ESP HTTP Client - ESP32-S3 - — ESP-IDF Programming Guide latest documentation
sources.quote: Official guide to sending HTTP and HTTPS requests from the ESP32-S3. Describes establishing a connection to a server in software, transmitting data and using a secure connection.

sources.title: ISO 41064:2023 — Health informatics — Standard communication protocol — Computer-assisted electrocardiography.
sources.quote: Official page for the standard governing the representation and exchange of digital ECG data, study information, measurements and interpretation results. The full text of the standard is available separately.

sources.title: DICOM PS3.3 — General ECG Information Object Definition.
sources.quote: Official DICOM specification for representing digitized electrical signals of the heart. Describes an ECG data object intended for exchange between compatible medical systems.

stickers.text:
We have identified possible ways of sending results to a physician, but wireless communication, the server and integration with a medical information system have not yet been implemented.

The ESP32-S3 microcontroller's support for BLE and Wi-Fi means only that data exchange is technically possible. Practical operation requires developing a transmission program and a receiving application or server, and checking the completeness of recordings and the protection of information.

Compliance with SCP-ECG or DICOM standards cannot be confirmed simply by saving data in XML or changing a file extension. The corresponding data structures must be implemented, and compatibility with the specific receiving system must be checked.

During laboratory development, we use synthetic recordings and fictitious identifiers. Transmitting real medical data will require compliance with the rules for protecting them and managing access. Remote analysis, including analysis using AI, does not replace confirmation of the device's diagnostic suitability.

The transmission path described is a proposed design scenario. The server, the physician's application and the secure data exchange have not yet been created.

Confirmation of delivery means that the receiving system has received and saved the data, but it does not prove their medical validity. Similarly, using HTTPS does not in itself resolve all issues concerning the protection of medical information: access management, protection of stored data and software security testing are also required separately.

The laboratory scenario should be tested only with synthetic recordings and fictitious identifiers.

stickers.title: Technical Clarification: The Path of One Recording from the Device to the Physician
stickers.text:
Let us consider one specific way of transmitting the results of our educational study, without attempting to implement all the communication options provided for in the technical specification at once.

Suppose the electrocardiograph has acquired a synthetic ECG lasting 10 seconds. The study has been assigned the identifier TEST-001, and the computer program has saved all 5000 samples and the necessary information about the recording.

At the first stage, the ESP32-S3 sends the results to the computer via USB. The computer program checks the sequence of samples, creates the study files and saves them.

We now need to send the study to a remote server. To do this, the program establishes a secure HTTPS connection, authenticates the server and sends the file together with the study identifier.

The server receives the data, checks that their structure is correct and saves the recording. After successfully saving it, the server sends a confirmation containing the identifier of the accepted study.

The computer program receives this confirmation and marks the recording as transmitted. If the connection is interrupted or no confirmation is received, the study must not be considered successfully delivered. Repeat transmission must be provided for in a way that prevents repeated requests from creating multiple copies of the same study.

To allow a physician to review the result, the server is to provide an application with access permissions. An authorized user selects study TEST-001, opens the cardiogram and, if necessary, obtains the original digital data.

Later, we can change the first stage of transmission. Instead of USB, the electrocardiograph will be able to use BLE to send the recording to a smartphone. The smartphone application will then be responsible for sending the study to the server. Another option is to use Wi-Fi, with the ESP32-S3 connecting to the server on its own.

However, changing the connection method must not change the content of the transmitted study. The identifier, sequence of samples, recording conditions and quality information must be preserved regardless of how they are transmitted.

Thus, the need to deliver medical information to a physician leads to the creation of a coordinated system in which the device, receiving application and server interact. But practical compatibility with a specific medical information system will additionally require implementing the exchange rules and data formats it supports.

content_json.html:
We have determined how the electrocardiograph will measure the electrical activity of the heart, save the results and send them to a physician. However, our laboratory system still depends on external power and consists of separate electronic boards. To use the device outside the laboratory, we need to enable it to operate independently and combine its components in a portable device.

Let us begin with the power supply. Certain voltages must be maintained for the ADS1291 and ESP32-S3 to operate. Previously, we used external power, but for the portable device we provide for a rechargeable battery — a source of electrical energy that can be recharged.

As the battery discharges, its voltage changes. Meanwhile, the electronic components require voltages within specified limits. The battery therefore cannot be regarded as a direct replacement for a regulated power supply. Voltage conversion and regulation must be provided so that each part of the device receives a suitable power supply.

In addition, the battery must be charged safely. For this, we use a specialized charge management system that controls the electrical current, voltage and charging conditions, and also provides protection for the battery against dangerous operating conditions. In accordance with the technical specification, we provide for a USB-C connector for connecting external power and charging.

But connecting a charger creates an additional electrical connection to external equipment. The power supply system must therefore not only enable independent operation but also continue to meet the electrical safety requirements discussed earlier. For medical use, safety will need to be confirmed separately both during battery operation and in the intended modes of connection to external power.

We now need to determine the battery operating time. To do this, we measure the electrical current consumed by the entire system during ECG recording, data storage and wireless transmission. Knowing the average current consumption and the available battery capacity allows us to make a preliminary estimate of the operating time. However, actual battery life must be checked experimentally, since consumption changes depending on the actions being performed.

It remains to combine the electronic components in an enclosure. We place the measurement board, microcontroller, power supply system, battery and necessary connectors inside it. The enclosure must protect the components from damage and accidental contact with electrical connections. Its design also determines the device's ease of use, dimensions and mass.

For the first laboratory prototype, we can retain the ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 development board. However, for a more compact device, we will later need to consider a custom printed circuit board combining the necessary components.

Thus, we are moving from a laboratory measurement system to the design of a standalone portable electrocardiograph. But having all the necessary parts does not yet prove that the device performs its functions correctly and safely. The next process is therefore to check the device we have created for compliance with the technical specification.
content_json.title: Creating a Portable Electrocardiograph
content_json.author: ai_checked

sources.title: Texas Instruments — BQ2407x Standalone 1-Cell 1.5-A Linear Battery Charger with PowerPath Datasheet (Rev. N).
sources.quote: Official documentation for the family of charge controllers. Describes charge management, power distribution between the device and the battery, temperature monitoring and protection functions. Provided as an example of a technical solution, not as the final component choice.

sources.title: Espressif — ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 v1.1 User Guide.
sources.quote: Official documentation for the development board. The Hardware Reference section explains power supply methods, the operation of the built-in voltage regulator and component locations. Used to determine the power requirements of the laboratory version of the ECG device.

stickers.text:
The card defines the principle for creating a portable device, but a specific battery power system has not yet been selected or designed.

The ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 board supports external power via USB, but the presence of a USB connector does not mean that it includes a battery charging system. A standalone version will require a separate charge management solution, a check of power source compatibility and testing.

For the laboratory prototype, only ready-made protected power sources intended for this purpose should be used, under an instructor's supervision. Modifying battery cells yourself is not required.

The dimensions, mass and battery operating time have not yet been determined. They can only be established after selecting the components, developing the design and taking measurements.

Portability does not confirm the device's medical safety. Until the necessary tests have been completed, it must not be used on a person.

stickers.title: Technical Clarification: Calculating Power Supply Requirements and Battery Life
stickers.text:
To determine a suitable battery capacity, we first need to find out how much electrical energy the device consumes.

The ESP32-S3's consumption is not constant: it changes when performing computations and using wireless communication. The ADS1291 and the other electronic components also consume energy. The calculation must therefore account for the entire system, not just the microcontroller.

Let us consider a hypothetical example. Suppose the electrocardiograph's average power consumption is 0.6 W.

For the calculation, we select a battery with a nominal voltage of 3.7 V and a capacity of 1000 mAh, or 1 Ah. Its nominal energy is 3.7 × 1 = 3.7 Wh.

But not all of the battery's energy reaches the electronic components. Some is lost during voltage conversion. If we assume an overall power supply system efficiency of 80%, we obtain 3.7 × 0.8 = 2.96 Wh of usable energy.

Let us divide this value by the average power consumption: 2.96 / 0.6 ≈ 4.9 hours.

Thus, under the hypothetical conditions selected, the device could operate for approximately five hours. The actual time will depend on real consumption, battery characteristics, temperature, allowable depth of discharge and wireless transmission modes.

The final choice of battery can therefore be made only after measuring the energy consumption of the working prototype.

In addition, we need to distinguish between the power source, the charge management system and the voltage regulators. The battery stores energy, the charge controller manages its replenishment, and the regulators produce the voltages required by the ADS1291 and ESP32-S3.

The USB-C connector provides the cable connection specified by the design, but it is not in itself a charging or electrical protection system. For a medical device, safe conditions for operation with external power, including charging mode, must be defined separately.

Finally, after selecting the components, we need to determine the dimensions and mass of the enclosure, position the boards and battery inside it, and provide access to the connectors and protection for the electronic parts.

Thus, portability is determined by more than the presence of a battery. It results from the coordinated operation of the power supply system, measurement electronics, software and device design.

content_json.title: Testing the Electrocardiograph We Have Created and Resolving the Contradiction

content_json.html:
We have defined the design of the portable electrocardiograph and the methods for measuring and processing the ECG, saving results, and transmitting them. However, having all the specified components does not yet mean that they work correctly together. We now need to test the system we have created and establish how closely its characteristics meet the technical specifications.

To do this, we carry out acceptance testing—a sequence of checks in which we compare the device's actual operation with requirements established in advance. Until the device's safety has been confirmed, we perform all tests on a laboratory test bench using artificial electrical signals.

We begin with voltage measurement accuracy. We connect a verified source that reproduces a known signal, for example with an amplitude of 1 mV, to the measurement system. We obtain an ECG recording and compare the measured amplitude with the specified amplitude. The difference between them indicates the measurement error. We repeat the check at several voltage values within the intended measurement range.

Next, we check the timing characteristics. At a sampling rate of 500 Hz, the device should acquire 5000 samples in 10 seconds and 15 000 in 30 seconds. Using the sequential numbers and acquisition times of the data, we establish whether any individual samples have been missed and whether the actual sampling rate matches the set rate.

To check the HR calculation, the simulator reproduces an ECG with a known frequency of cardiac cycles, for example 60 and 90 per minute. The program identifies QRS complexes, calculates the intervals between them, and calculates HR. We compare the result with the specified value and, if errors are detected, determine whether they arose during measurement or software processing.

We now investigate the effects of interference. First, we measure the device's own noise level with a constant input signal. Then, using laboratory equipment intended for these checks, we assess input impedance, common-mode interference rejection, and resistance to external electrical effects. We compare the characteristics obtained with the requirements for the device under development.

After this, we check the digital filters. We compare the original and processed recordings under various artificially generated types of interference. We record how much the unwanted fluctuations have decreased and how the shape of the desired signal has changed. We separately check whether the filters can be disabled and adjusted.

We also need to make sure that the device can recognize certain measurement problems. Using a laboratory simulator, we check detection of a broken connection corresponding to electrode disconnection and the appearance of a warning about poor signal quality.

Finally, we check saving and transmitting the study. We create a recording lasting 10–30 seconds, save it in the specified formats, open the resulting files, and compare their contents with the original data. When transmitting over USB, BLE, or Wi-Fi, we check the completeness of the received recording and the program's response to an interrupted connection. For the portable version, we additionally measure battery operating time.

Thus, we move from an idea of how the electrocardiograph should work to verifiable results of its operation. But even successful completion of functional testing does not confirm that the device is safe for people and can be used in medicine. This requires a separate check of compliance with safety requirements and regulatory documents.

stickers.text:
The card describes an acceptance testing program, but does not contain results from actually carrying out the tests.

For a final assessment, permissible errors and limit values for the characteristics must be established in advance, as these are not fully specified in the original technical specifications. Verified measuring equipment, test methods, and reports containing actual results will also be needed.

An ECG simulator allows the main measurement and software functions to be checked, but does not replace specialized electrical and electromagnetic safety testing.

In particular, testing protection against defibrillator pulses requires special equipment and trained specialists. It must not be carried out using an actual defibrillator on an ordinary student test bench.

Until safety has been confirmed, testing is performed exclusively with artificial signals, without connecting a person.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: how to document the results of acceptance tes
stickers.text:
For acceptance testing, it is necessary to define in advance what result counts as successful. Otherwise, we may obtain many measurements but will not be able to establish whether the device meets the technical specifications.

For each requirement, we record five pieces of information: what we are checking, what value is required, how the check is performed, what result was actually obtained, and whether the requirement has been met.

For example, when checking amplitude, we use a laboratory signal source with known characteristics. If the specified amplitude is 1.00 mV and the device displays 0.98 mV, the deviation is −0.02 mV, or −2%.

But this can only be called a successful result if the permissible error has been defined in advance and the actual deviation is within its limits.

To check HR, we use an artificial cardiogram with a known frequency of cardiac cycles set in advance. For example, we set 60 and 90 cycles per minute. We compare the program's results with these values and record QRS complex detection errors.

To check recording, we set a sampling rate of 500 Hz and a duration of 10 seconds. We expect to obtain 5000 samples, but separately check the actual recording time and the absence of data loss.

To check filtering, we compare the original and processed signals. We need to establish not only the reduction in interference, but also the change in the desired ECG waveform.

To check data transmission, we compare the study before sending it and after it is received by the receiving program. We check the number of samples, their sequence, the study identifier, and the response to an interrupted connection.

Separate tests must cover input impedance, CMRR, noise level, electrode lead-off detection, and other specified characteristics of the measurement system.

If an actual result has not yet been obtained, we enter “Not tested” in the report. If the check has been performed but the requirements have not been met, we enter “Does not comply” and a description of the deviation detected. If the technical specifications do not include a permissible value for a characteristic, we record the need to establish an acceptance criterion.

Thus, acceptance testing turns a list of proposed functions into a system of verifiable requirements. Its results show which properties of the device have actually been confirmed and which still need to be achieved.

content_json.html:
We have defined the procedure for checking the electrocardiograph's measurement and software functions. However, even if the device correctly reproduces the cardiogram, calculates HR, and transmits results to a doctor, this does not yet mean that it can be connected to a person.

Let us return to the opposing process—ensuring human safety. This is what required the device being created not only to obtain information about the heart's activity, but also to prevent dangerous effects on the body. We now need to confirm that the protective measures we have specified actually work.

To do this, we first consider possible hazards throughout the device's use. For example, a power supply fault may cause unwanted voltage to appear on the electrodes, damaged insulation may create a dangerous path for electric current, and a software error may lead to an incorrect measurement result. For each hazard, we identify possible consequences, assess the risk, provide ways to reduce it, and check their effectiveness.

This approach is called medical device risk management. Its principles are established by the international standard ISO 14971. Importantly, safety is determined not by the presence of individual protective components, but by the results of testing the entire system under the intended operating conditions and possible faults.

The requirements of IEC 60601-1 apply to medical electrical equipment. They cover basic electrical safety and maintenance of the device's essential functions. Therefore, protection against dangerous currents, electrical insulation, power supply safety, and device operation under specified fault conditions must be professionally tested.

But electrical effects can not only harm a person; they can also disrupt the operation of the electrocardiograph itself. For example, external electromagnetic interference can distort measurements or cause a software failure. Therefore, IEC 60601-1-2 also applies, establishing requirements and tests related to electromagnetic effects.

Materials that come into contact with the human body, particularly electrodes, require separate assessment. It is necessary to make sure that they do not create unacceptable biological risks for the intended manner and duration of contact. The ISO 10993 series of standards is used for this assessment.

Safety also depends on the software. For example, the program must not lose measurement results without notice, determine HR incorrectly, or report good signal quality when a fault has been detected. Therefore, medical software development includes documenting requirements, testing program operation, and managing errors. The corresponding processes are addressed in IEC 62304.

If the electrocardiograph is intended for continuous ambulatory monitoring, the applicability of the specific requirements of IEC 60601-2-47 must also be determined. For a device that makes individual short ECG recordings, the applicability of this standard cannot be established solely on the basis of its portability.

After development and the necessary testing have been completed, the device's eligibility for medical use must be confirmed through the procedure established by law. For Kazakhstan, this means determining the device's intended purpose and risk class, preparing technical and registration documentation, undergoing the required expert assessment, and obtaining state registration. Common rules for the circulation of medical devices apply within the EAEU, while registration under national rules remains possible during the transition period.

Thus, ensuring safety ceases to be merely a requirement that constrains electrical measurement. It determines the design, software, testing, and conditions for medical use of the device created.

But until the listed checks have been performed and compliance with the requirements has been confirmed, all we have is a design for a laboratory prototype electrocardiograph. Only confirmation of the necessary characteristics and safety allows us to move toward resolution of the original contradiction.
content_json.title: Confirming the safety of the medical device
content_json.author: ai_checked

stickers.text:
The card defines the main areas for confirming the safety of a medical electrocardiograph, but this does not mean that the corresponding tests have been performed or that the device complies with the specified standards.

Practical confirmation will require establishing the device's exact intended medical purpose, the applicable regulatory requirements, and acceptable risk levels. The protective circuits, software, and entire design must then be developed and tested, the required tests performed, and their results documented.

International standards do not replace state registration of a medical device. The applicability of particular editions of standards and the registration procedure are determined by the requirements of the relevant jurisdiction.

Until these conditions have been met, the design we have created can only be regarded as a laboratory prototype for research using artificial signals, not as a device authorized for medical use.

stickers.title: Technical clarification: what evidence is needed for confirma
stickers.text:
To confirm the safety of a medical electrocardiograph, testing individual electronic components is not enough. It is necessary to define the intended purpose of the finished device, identify hazards, and collect evidence that the device maintains the required characteristics under the intended operating conditions.

First, we establish exactly what the device is intended for. For example, a device for short-term recording of one lead for rhythm screening and a device for producing a diagnostic ECG report may fall within different scopes of specific standards. The necessary checks and registration documentation also depend on the intended purpose.

We then consider the risks that arise when using the device.

Electrical risk: a power supply or insulation fault may lead to dangerous effects through the electrodes. Protective measures must be defined and the results of the specified tests obtained.

Measurement risk: interference, overload, or poor electrode contact can distort the cardiogram. It is necessary to check whether the device maintains the required measurement quality and detects the specified faults.

Software risk: a data processing error may lead to an incorrect HR, loss of a recording, or incorrect presentation of results. Software requirements must be defined, its functions tested, and detected errors documented.

Biological risk: materials that come into contact with the skin may have unwanted effects. Their suitability for the intended conditions and duration of contact must be assessed.

Risk of a confidentiality breach: information about the study and the patient may become accessible to unauthorized persons. Therefore, data protection during storage and transmission must be checked.

For each risk, we define the measures provided to reduce it, the verification method, and the actual result. If the risk remains unacceptable, the design or conditions of use of the device must be changed and the corresponding checks repeated.

After development is complete, we assemble the technical documentation: the device's intended purpose, circuit diagrams, component information, software requirements, measurement test results, and documents on risk management and safety confirmation.

Next, we establish the applicable regulatory requirements and the procedure for authorizing the device for medical use. For Kazakhstan, the legislation of the Republic of Kazakhstan and the current EAEU rules for medical device registration must be taken into account.

Thus, resolution of the contradiction requires not only creating a working electrocardiograph, but also demonstrating that medical information is obtained at a confirmed level of safety. Until such evidence is available, the result of development remains a laboratory prototype.

content_json.html:
We began with the need to develop a way to obtain reliable information about the functioning of the human heart for medical purposes. Studying the electrical activity of the heart led us to measure the potential difference between points on the surface of the body, and then to create an electronic device capable of recording changes in this voltage.

However, obtaining a signal requires an electrical connection to a person, which under certain conditions may harm their health. This is how we identified the opposing process—ensuring the person's safety. It requires obtaining information about the functioning of the heart to preserve health, but at the same time prevents the use of a device whose safety has not been confirmed.

The contradiction lay in the creation of the electrocardiograph itself, as a unity of the development of these two processes. We needed to expand the capabilities of electrical measurement while simultaneously limiting the dangers arising from carrying it out.

The development of this contradiction determined the sequence of steps in creating the instrument. The need to begin measurements safely led to the use of an ECG simulator. The need to obtain reliable information led to the development of a measurement system, conversion of voltage into numbers, software processing, and signal quality control. The need to use the results led to their storage and transmission to a physician.

At the same time, safety requirements changed the design of the device itself. Protection of the measurement inputs, a safe power supply, electrical isolation, and fault detection had to be provided. These solutions, in turn, required checking their effect on measurement accuracy. Therefore, obtaining information and ensuring safety cannot be implemented independently of each other by simply connecting ready-made parts.

The resolution of the contradiction is the creation of a single-channel electrocardiograph in which reliable measurement of the electrical activity of the heart and the person's safety are ensured within a single device. The instrument does not eliminate the need for electrical interaction with a person, but makes such interaction permissible through specially created and verified conditions.

This transition represents a qualitative leap: instead of separate technical solutions, a new whole emerges—a medical device capable of acquiring, processing, storing, and transmitting information about the functioning of the heart with confirmed compliance with safety requirements.

However, such a qualitative leap cannot be considered to have occurred merely because an electronic circuit has been assembled and an ECG recording has been obtained on a laboratory test bench. To complete the creation of a medical device, it is necessary to confirm its measurement characteristics, the effectiveness of its protective solutions, and compliance with applicable regulatory requirements, as well as to complete the necessary procedures for approval for medical use.

Thus, the laboratory prototype is a stage in the development of the contradiction, while the finished single-channel electrocardiograph with confirmed characteristics and safety is its resolution.
content_json.title: Resolution of the contradiction — creating a single-channel electrocardiograph
